title: Beatrix and the Visitor
premise: Folklorist Marguerite Underhill returns to her grandmother's decaying house in the village of Hollowmere to catalog songs no one will sing twice, only to find that every photograph taken there now includes an empty chair that shouldn't exist. The chair belongs to something the villagers took in 1974—a child-sized visitor from beneath the mere, traded away for the village's survival—and it has spent fifty years learning to sit where it was promised a place. As Marguerite records the forbidden songs, she realizes she was the collateral of that bargain: the child who was allowed to live invisible so long as she never looked back. To survive, she must return what was taken—her own name, given to the thing in 1974 by her grandmother—before the last surviving elder signs the house over and dissolves the boundary holding the visitor at bay. In the end, Marguerite gives up her identity willingly, becoming the village's new keeper while the visitor finally takes its chair, and the found family of Hollowmere's outcasts buries the bargain for good.
about_author: Jonah Ishikawa is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloging oral histories in coastal English villages before turning to fiction. They write horror about inheritance, bargains, and the things families agree not to discuss.

chapters.title: The Chair That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Marguerite arrives at her grandmother's shuttered house to settle the estate and record local songs. Sorting photographs for the funeral, she notices an extra wooden chair appearing in images spanning decades—always empty, always closer to the camera. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: unease disguised as grief; the rational folklorist begins losing her grip on explanation.

chapters.title: Songs No One Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Marguerite interviews villagers for her folklore archive. Every singer cuts off mid-verse when they reach a line about 'the one below the water,' and old Tam Weller warns her some songs are contracts. She finds her grandmother's 1974 field notes, pages torn out. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into dread as patterns emerge.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Beneath loose floorboards, Marguerite discovers a box: a christening certificate bearing two names—hers and something unpronounceable—plus a photograph of her grandmother shaking hands with a figure half-submerged at the mere's edge. The chair appears in this photo too, occupied. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: betrayal; the woman who raised her made a deal.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Marguerite confronts Edith Crane, the final signatory on the house papers and the only villager who'll speak plainly. Edith reveals the 1974 bargain: the village fed the mere-thing a name instead of a child, and Marguerite was that child. The sale of the house ends the arrangement. POV: alternating Marguerite and Edith. Emotional beat: the price of survival named aloud.

chapters.title: Invisible by Design
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter through grandmother Agnes's 1974 diary entries interleaved with Marguerite's present. We learn how Agnes offered her granddaughter's name to spare her body, buying her a life of being overlooked—jobs lost, friendships faded, always forgotten. POV: Agnes (diary) framing Marguerite. Emotional beat: horrifying tenderness; protection as erasure.

chapters.title: It Learned to Sit
chapters.summary: The visitor crosses over early, sensing the coming dissolution. It manifests in the house—not violent, but terribly patient, arranging itself in photographs, warming the chair, mimicking Marguerite's childhood habits. Neighbors begin greeting her with a stranger's name. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: uncanny intimacy; the thing wants to be family, not enemy.

chapters.title: The Found Family of Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Marguerite bonds with the village's other overlooked ones—Tam, Edith, and the ferryman's mute daughter—who were all touched by older bargains. Together they decipher the torn song verses: the full ballad is a return ritual requiring a willing surrender of identity. POV: ensemble, anchored in Marguerite. Emotional beat: warmth amid horror; belonging found exactly where she was erased.

chapters.title: Signing Day
chapters.summary: Edith, dying, prepares to sign the papers; solicitors arrive as the mere rises into the garden. The boundary thins—shadows move wrong, the house fills with the smell of deep water. The visitor stands at Marguerite's shoulder, waiting politely for what it believes is owed. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: rising panic; time collapses to hours.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: At the mere's edge, Marguerite sings the completed ballad and speaks her true name—the one buried since 1974—surrendering it willingly rather than letting it be taken. The visitor receives the name, sits at last in its chair within the water, and the bargain closes on terms the village never intended. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: climax; grief and agency fused in sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Keeper of Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Nameless but known, Marguerite stays as the house's new keeper, held in memory by her found family even though records forget her. The photographs now show an empty chair by choice, kept set for whoever comes next. Edith's papers are burned unsigned. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; identity lost, family chosen, survival paid in full.
